nameStory: The scientific name 'lamellosus' comes from the Latin word for 'layered' or 'plated,' likely referring to some structural feature of this spider's anatomy. Since this species lacks a widely-used common name, it's typically referred to simply as a funnel weaver, named for the characteristic funnel-shaped webs that all members of this family create.
description: Coras lamellosus is a funnel weaver spider that builds the classic sheet webs with funnel retreats that you might spot in corners of buildings or natural crevices. Like other funnel weavers, it has a moderately robust body with long, sturdy legs that help it run quickly across its web surface. These spiders are typically brown or grayish in coloration with subtle patterns that help them blend into their surroundings. They're medium-sized spiders, neither tiny nor particularly large compared to other common New England species.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Look for a flat, sheet-like web with a distinctive funnel-shaped retreat at one corner where the spider hides - the web feels slightly sticky but not as clingy as an orb weaver's web

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Moderately chunky body with a slightly flattened appearance and long, powerful-looking legs that seem built for speed rather than delicate web work

idTips.label: Markings
idTips.description: Generally brown or gray coloration with subtle darker patterns - not boldly marked but with enough variation to break up the spider's outline

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Sits hidden in the funnel retreat and darts out lightning-fast when prey hits the web, then quickly drags it back to the safety of the funnel

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Eight eyes arranged in two rows, giving the spider decent vision for detecting movement both on the web and in the surrounding area

habitat: Found in various sheltered locations including rock crevices, under logs, in building corners, and other protected spots where they can anchor their funnel webs. They prefer areas with some moisture and protection from direct weather exposure. Look for them in woodlands, around human structures, and in natural rock formations.

seasonality.spring: Adults become active as temperatures warm, beginning to build or repair their funnel webs in suitable locations.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to spot these spiders and their characteristic funnel webs in full form.
seasonality.fall: Still active but preparing for winter - webs may become less maintained as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters in protected locations, with webs either abandoned or significantly reduced in maintenance.

funFact: Funnel weaver spiders can run across their webs at speeds that would be equivalent to a human sprinting at over 30 miles per hour - they're among the fastest spiders in North America when moving across their silky highways!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other funnel weaver species, especially grass spiders that build similar webs in gardens. The key difference is location - Coras species typically build in more sheltered, protected spots like rock crevices rather than openly in grass or shrubs.
contextualKnowledge: The genus name 'Coras' doesn't have an obvious meaning to most people, but it helps distinguish this group from the more familiar grass spider funnel weavers that people commonly encounter in their yards.
compareHints: Distinguishing between different Coras species requires close examination of anatomical features that are difficult to see in the field. Coras lamellosus is separated from its relatives like Coras medicinalis and the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver mainly by subtle differences in reproductive structures and specific habitat preferences. For field identification, focus on the funnel web structure and general habitat rather than trying to distinguish between Coras species.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Distinguishing Coras medicinalis from its close relatives like Coras lamellosus or the Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver requires examining fine details of body structure that are difficult to see in the field.

The Northern Spurred Woodland Funnelweaver can be distinguished from its Coras relatives primarily by the male's distinctive leg spurs and its preference for higher elevation, cooler woodland habitats.
Distinguishing Coras juvenilis from its close relatives like Coras medicinalis or Coras montanus requires expert examination of reproductive structures and other microscopic features.
Coras aerialis is virtually indistinguishable in the field from its relatives like Coras medicinalis and Coras montanus without examining reproductive structures under magnification.
